reasoning: All 7 failure edits were kept, with the corrective wording intact. Of the 6 success edits, 5 stand alone and 1 was merged into a failure edit. The only overlap was that the failure 'list of real people' edit and the success 'Title / rank / role held by A, B & C' edit both used the same insert_after target. I merged them into one edit, kept as failure, with support 3. I added a qualifier so the two don't contradict each other: the shared country, state or team applies to bare lists of people, and the shared role noun applies only when the clue explicitly asks for a title, rank, position or role. The other success edits (paraphrase matching, flashcard layouts, appositive and converging passages, stage-direction, wordplay-check and definition clues, and film title is the object) target different anchors and cover patterns the failure edits do not address, so they were kept. No edit touches the protected SLOW_UPDATE section.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content:
This also holds for a bare comma-separated list or pair of real people with no verb ('Ferdinand VII, Juan Carlos'; 'Princess Caroline & Princess Stephanie'; kings, presidents, senators, players). The answer is the ONE shared proper noun the passages tie them to: for monarchs or heads of state the country or realm ('Spain', 'Monaco'); for legislators the state; for athletes the team; otherwise the family, band or similar group. The answer is never one list member, a regnal variant of one ('Juan Carlos I'), a third person from the same passages, or a relationship/descriptor word such as 'sisters', 'brothers', 'actors' or 'princesses'.
- Exception: when the clue itself asks for a 'title / rank / position / role held by A, B & C' (people from different countries or eras, 'Balbinus, Bao Dai & Bidatsu'), the answer is the ONE role noun they all share ('Emperor'). Give it bare and singular, without a country or 'of ...' tail, and do not answer with one of the named people.

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content: - An acronym or abbreviation inside the clue ('If your TV has PIP, it has this feature', 'DVR', 'GPS') usually means the answer is the spelled-out expansion ('Picture in Picture'). Look for the passages that gloss the letters ('Picture in Picture (PIP)') and answer with that expansion. Ignore unrelated phrases from forum threads or questions that merely sit next to the acronym.

edits.target: Other named entities in the clue are anchors, never the answer.
edits.content:
- A clue whose subject is only a pronoun with a dated action ('On June 16, 1881 he wrote an explanation of why he was going to kill President Garfield', 'In 1815 she ...') asks for WHO that person is, as a bare name ('Charles Guiteau'). Never answer with a document, poem, speech or other work the person produced, or with an event. Passages often mention several things he wrote or did, and those are only details to identify him. Pick the name that every passage ties to the clue's date and action.
- The answer's category is set by the clue's noun or pronoun, not by the dominant topic of the passages. 'Water is lost through this PART of the tree' -> a part ('leaves'), not the process the passages discuss ('transpiration'). 'THEY were once called "Saratoga Chips" after the town where they were first made' -> the thing that bore the old name ('Potato chips'), not the town named in the clue ('Saratoga Springs'). With a pronoun subject ('they', 'it', 'these'), the answer is the generic object being described. Places, processes and people named in the clue are anchors.

edits.target: for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - Apply the bare-word test strictly and do NOT repeat the type noun the clue already supplies ('this mint', 'these mountains', 'this gift company', 'this term'). If a trivia answer key would accept the bare name, give only the bare name: 'this mint whose mark is a "D"' -> 'Denver' (not 'Denver Mint'); 'this gift company' -> 'Hallmark' (not 'Hallmark Cards'; always drop Cards/Inc/Co./Corp./Company); 'Lake Placid is in these mountains' -> 'Adirondacks' (ranges take their short plural name: Rockies, Alps, Andes, Adirondacks, not 'Adirondack Mountains'). Also drop clue-supplied anchor words from a term: 'the term for the passing of Venus in front of the sun' -> 'Transit' (not 'Transit of Venus'). Keep a head noun only when the bare word names a different thing (Roman Empire, hydrogen bomb).

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Person names: default to 'First Last' with no middle initial, middle name or generational suffix ('Lyndon Johnson', not 'Lyndon B. Johnson'; 'George Bush', not 'George H. W. Bush'). Keep an initial only if a verbatim archive answer in the context shows it, or the name is almost never written without it ('John F. Kennedy').

edits.target: Brief reasoning belongs before the tags.
edits.content:
- Ordinals, numbers and role words that the clue already uses for the referent ('The THIRD leader of the Yellow Hat sect was the first to bear this title') are not part of the answer. Give the bare title or name ('Dalai Lama', not 'third Dalai Lama'). This covers 'first/second/third', 'the 14th', and 'former/late'.
- Completing a quotation or line of verse ('... to wash the steps with pail and' this): answer with only the missing word, cleanly spelled ('rag'). If one passage shows a typo or stray characters ('ragaE', a footnote mark, or a line number glued to the word), compare it with the other passages that quote the line and drop the artifact. Never answer with a longer phrase than the single missing word unless the gap clearly spans several words.

## Rule 5: Wordplay clues that show the garbled version
- Spoonerism clues ('Dr. Spooner once talked of his queer old dean', 'He toasted the "queer old dean"') display what was mis-spoken. The answer is the INTENDED phrase obtained by swapping the initial sounds back ('dear old queen'). Give the complete intended phrase (all the words that were swapped), not just one swapped word ('queen'), and do not repeat the garbled phrase. Passages usually gloss it ('instead of "our dear old Queen"'), so copy that gloss without the lead-in words ('our', 'a toast to').
- Other clues that quote a mangled saying, pun or misspoken phrase ask for the original correct version in the same way.

edits.target: A phrase repeated across independent passages is strong evidence.
edits.content: - The passage sentence is often a PARAPHRASE of the clue, not a copy. Match on the clue's verbs and objects ('run out of ... mix lipstick with petroleum jelly' ~ 'If you've run out of blush, mix a little lipstick with Vaseline and apply it to your cheeks'). Read off the word in the slot, then check that it fits the clue's category noun ('cheek cosmetic' -> 'blush'). Answer with that bare common noun.

edits.target: - Archive lines may also be formatted 'CATEGORY | clue text | answer'. Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content:
- Flashcard dumps (StudyStack and similar) run cards together in ALL CAPS: 'CLUE TEXT, ANSWER. NEXT CARD CLUE...'. The answer is the short phrase between the end of the clue and the next period ('...INTO THIS LANGUAGE, WELSH. POLAND'S...' -> Welsh; '..."I KNOW THIS MUCH IS TRUE", WALLY LAMB. THERE'S NO...' -> Wally Lamb). Ignore the text after that period because it belongs to another card. Write the answer in normal capitalisation, without the clue words.
- Flashcard and timeline snippets may have no '|' separator at all. The clue words may run straight into the answer after a trailing list or ellipsis ('...THE TATE GALLERY, UNESCO IN PARIS, AND LINCOLN CENTER, HENRY MOORE'), or the layout may be answer-first ('Casimir Pulaski Polish count who organized an independent cavalry corps...'). In both cases take the proper name or term sitting at the boundary of the matched clue text, and confirm it against the other passages.

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - Appositive hits and converging passages are strong evidence. When the clue's descriptors ('famed horticulturist ... Santa Rosa plum', 'favorite rifle ... Tick-Licker') or ALL of its anchors (film + actor, county + landmark, song + singer) appear in several independent passages right next to one proper noun, answer with it right away and do not search for a trickier alternative. Give a person's standard full name as the passages use it ('Luther Burbank', 'Stuart Sutcliffe'), not a nickname ('Stu') or a bare surname. Crossword-solver pages that only echo the clue, or add hints such as '5 letter, 2nd letter O', are not answer sources. Use their length and letter hints only to check a candidate.

edits.target: answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content:
- Leading stage-direction parentheticals ('(Schumacher reads his clue.)', '(Jimmy of the Clue Crew ...)') are also filler. Ignore them and answer from the factual core of the clue.
- Wordplay or descriptive adjectives in the clue ('alliterative bassist', 'nightmarish singer', 'looks nothing like Kevin Sorbo') are not the answer, but they are a cheap CHECK on your candidate. Prefer the candidate that fits them (S-S: Stuart Sutcliffe; Sorbo played Hercules, so the constellation is Hercules). If a passage puts the joke's name next to a candidate, that confirms it.
- Definition or etymology clues ('It's in dictionaries as the sound a small object makes dropping into water', 'paper-thin pastry whose name is Greek for "leaf"') ask for the HEADWORD that a dictionary or encyclopedia snippet defines in nearly the clue's wording ('Plop - definition of plop...'). Answer with that headword in the form the passages repeat ('plop', 'phyllo'). Do not answer with a word from inside the definition ('splash', 'dough'). If the passages show spelling variants, use the most common English spelling.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - 'Colin Farrell trapped in one of these' / 'the movie with X stuck in one of these': the clue describes a film or book whose own title often names the object ('Phone Booth'). Find the passage about that work (its title or first sentence repeats the actor, director and plot) and answer with the object term from the title, with no 'film' or year.
